schools.summary: Gill distinguishes the mockers from the aged friends: not men of mean birth but a set of profligate wretches whose derision, coming from juniors and inferiors, is the sharpest aggravation of a good man's affliction.

Clarke sets the verse against ch. 29:8 — the youth who once revered him now scorn him, reckoning him beneath the 'dogs of my flock,' an expression of sovereign contempt; Wesley marks that nature itself taught the young to reverence their elders.

Ellicott renders 'whose fathers I disdained to set' as a plain past fact; Keil and Delitzsch frame the reversal — the man once an object of reverential fear to the city's youth is now the sport of its vagabonds.

Henry opens the complaint of the meanness of the persons who affront him, and guards that Job 'speaks of what he might have done, not of what he did,' too mindful of human dignity actually to set men with his dogs.

debates.question: Did Job actually disdain the fathers of these men, or only speak of what he might have done?

sides.position: A suppressed wish — what Job might have done, not what he did
A plain past fact — Job actually disdained to set their fathers with his dogs

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch note the long opening line as a deep, long-breathed start to the lament and the particle 'but now' as the turning-point; Ellicott fixes the fathers as the subject here, the children in what follows, and likens the tribe to Herodotus' Troglodytes.
Gill reads the worthless strength of men so slothful they kept it only to fold their hands, unfit for any profitable business.
Clarke glosses 'their old age also has perished' — the strength unesteemed in youth, the age without honour — and records Good's proposal that the words are Arabic.
Henry gathers both generations as the unprofitable burdens of the earth: the young unfit for labour, the old 'twice children,' their old age perished.

outliers.note: Records Mr. Good's proposal that the verse's principal words are really Arabic and should be joined to the next verse: 'with whom crabbed looks are perpetual, from hunger and flinty famine.'

schools.summary: Gill reads the difficult word of a people reduced by famine to the utmost extremity, destitute as a rock or hard flint from which nothing can be got.
Keil and Delitzsch render them 'benumbed from want and hunger, who gnaw the steppe,' the desert their cheerless pasture.
Clarke takes 'fleeing into the wilderness' as the extreme of want; Wesley reads 'solitary' of men who from guilt shunned all company and fled to desolate places.
Henry: extremely poor, too proud to beg and too idle to dig, brought to their straits by sloth, so that none relieved them and they fled to the deserts for shelter and food.

debates.question: What is the sense of the word rendered 'solitary'?

sides.position: Reduced to a barren solitude, benumbed with famine like the flint
Deliberately shunning the eyes of men and fleeing from justice

themes: the wretched stock of the mockers

schools.summary: Gill rehearses the long dispute over the 'mallows' — not the common mallow but a salt herb, Broughton's 'salt herbs,' the sea-purslain the poor ate.
Keil and Delitzsch fix it as the tall shrubby orach whose buds the poor gather, citing the Talmudic tale of King Jannai serving these same mallows in memory of the fathers.

Clarke derives the word from 'salt' and labours the harder puzzle of the broom or juniper root, doubting whether its roots were eaten or its wood burned to bake bread, and settling it by Olaus Magnus; Wesley keeps 'bitter herbs' and owns the Hebrews at a loss over plant-names.

outliers.note: Cites the Gothic archbishop Olaus Magnus that among his own people the very roots of the juniper were eaten for bread in famine, to settle the doubt whether the juniper's roots were food or only its wood fuel (cf. the 'coals of juniper,' Ps. 120:4).

schools.summary: Gill: driven from all civil society as unfit, not for any good but for their crimes, like felons or transported men.
Clarke pictures men no one would employ, chased from the city with the hue and cry raised, and notes Good's alternative that they 'slunk away like a thief.'

Henry paints them the scum of the country — thieving, lurking, mischievous — rid from the land while the mob cried 'Away with such fellows,' yet justly reckoned thieves who steal by refusing honest labour.

debates.question: Does the last clause mean the outcasts were cried after, or that they slunk away?

sides.position: They were cried after, as a thief is
They slunk away, like a thief

schools.summary: Gill glosses the 'cliffs of the valleys' as the hollow places scooped by floods, into which these men crept for want of a roof.

Keil and Delitzsch identify the men as the same degraded rabble of the previous strophe, now viewed by their coarse manner of life, who make sport of Job when their marauding brings them onto his domain (cf. Job 24:4).
Clarke reads it of a people obliged to shelter in the most dangerous, out-of-the-way, and unfrequented places.

themes: caves and clefts of the rock
a people viewed by its baseness

schools.summary: Ellicott recalls Herodotus that such cave-dwellers' speech was like the screeching of bats, and insists the whole description is present tense — these are the very men now mocking Job; Keil and Delitzsch tell how naked and drenched they shift for themselves in every season.

Clarke has them cry among the bushes for food like the wild ass, records the manuscript variant 'they groaned' for 'they brayed,' and huddled under the brambles like beasts; Wesley: they brayed for hunger and hid under thorns from justice.
Gill hears men likened to wild asses, groaning through cold or want, since the wild ass 'brays not but when in want.'

debates.question: Do the outcasts 'bray' like beasts or 'groan' like broken men?

sides.position: 'They brayed' (yinhaku)
'They groaned' (yinaku), on two manuscripts

schools.summary: Gill weighs 'fools' not as idiots but as men of slender capacity, 'Nabal-like,' and leans to the stronger biblical sense of the wicked, shrewd enough for evil though dull to good.
Ellicott renders the close 'they are scourged out of the land'; Keil and Delitzsch keep the older 'viler than the earth.'
Clarke reads 'children of nabal, children without a name,' and prefers 'driven out of the land' to 'viler than the earth.'
Henry ends the catalogue on a nameless baseness — a kind without fame, banished as viler than the earth — and draws the thanksgiving that we are not such men.

debates.question: Does the last clause mean 'viler than the earth' or 'driven/scourged out of the land'?

sides.position: Viler than the earth itself
Scourged or driven out of the land, outcasts

themes: the depth of the mockers' descent

schools.summary: Gill hears Job made the very subject of their song, as the Psalmist was 'the song of the drunkards,' a byword handed round in the mouths of the base.
Clarke: 'I am the subject of their mirth, and serve as a proverb or by-word; they use me with every species of indignity.'
Keil and Delitzsch mark this as the second of the three 'but now' clauses that shape the elegy; Ellicott points to the margin as warrant for a Messianic reading of Job's complaints.

themes: the ruin of a good name

schools.summary: Gill: they abhorred him not for evil but for the good his integrity reproved, and for his meanness and disease — a type of Christ, whom the rulers abhorred, preferring a robber to him.
Keil and Delitzsch give the stark order — they abhor him, flee far, and withhold not their spittle from his face.

Clarke exclaims at a society that permits such indignities to the aged and afflicted; Wesley reads the 'spitting' figuratively, since they kept far off — every kind of reproach flung to his face, a type of Christ.

debates.question: Is the 'spitting' literal spittle or figurative reproach?

sides.position: Actual spittle, a gesture of loathing
Figurative — reproachful words flung in his face, since they kept far off

schools.summary: Gill spreads out the senses of 'my cord' (the Keri) — the loosened nerves, the untwisted estate, or best the cord of his magistracy — while noting the written text reads 'his cord.'

Clarke takes 'his cord' as God's bowstring, the archer loosing his arrow (cf. the Vulgate/LXX 'opened his quiver'), and the mockers casting off restraint like headstrong horses; Wesley: God slackened the string of his bow and loosed the bridle of their humanity.
Ellicott judges the written text better: 'God hath loosed the cord of his bow, and they have cast off all restraint before me.'

debates.question: Whose cord is loosed — Job's or God's?

sides.position: Job's own cord — his life, authority, or estate
God's bowstring, loosed to shoot Job and to loose the rabble upon him

schools.summary: Gill dwells on the word for the youths — young birds scarce out of the shell — who rose in hostility and took his right hand as though his betters, and rejects the reading 'the flower.'

Clarke renders the term 'younglings' and reads them tripping his heels and rolling on him like wave on wave; Wesley makes the right hand the accuser's place in court and the 'ways of destruction' the siege-banks cast up against him.
Ellicott: 'the youth' are the young brood, the rabble; Keil and Delitzsch join the verse to the sustained assault of the rabble pressing his right and thrusting his feet away.
Gill reads 'mar my path' inwardly, of men hindering Job's religion and reproaching his holy walk.

Clarke keeps the siege: they destroy the way-marks as besiegers break the roads, and (with Good) 'have no adviser'; Wesley makes them stop all Job's ways of escape and swell his calamity with their censures, 'even they' who are themselves miserable.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'they tear down my path' and 'minister to my overthrow, they who themselves are helpless'; Ellicott takes 'no helper' to mean they gain no advantage by their malice.

debates.question: What does 'they have no helper' mean?

sides.position: The tormentors are themselves helpless, having no adviser
They gain no help or advantage by their malice

schools.summary: Gill draws out the double image — a breach in the sea-banks and a breach in a besieged wall — through which Job's enemies pour and bear down all before them, wallowing in the ruin.

Keil and Delitzsch tie the 'breach' to Job's earlier 'breach upon breach' (Job 16:14), the wall already broken by God's decrees; Ellicott offers 'as through a wide breach they come; in the midst of the crash they roll themselves upon me.'
Clarke reads the siege in sequence — sap, breach, storm, flight, pursuit — the assailants rolling in as an irresistible torrent.

debates.question: How is the difficult word ('in the desolation') to be rendered?

sides.position: 'In the desolation' they roll themselves upon me
'Under the crash' of the falling wall, or 'instead of a tempest'

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch mark this as the third and last 'but now' that reopens the elegy, terrors pursuing 'my nobility like the wind, and like a cloud my prosperity passed away.'
Gill is careful the terrors are not those of a guilty conscience, a condemning law, death, or judgment — Job's conscience was clear — but the terrors of God's afflicting hand now turned against him.
Henry calls the terror of the soul the sorest part of the calamity: pursued as by the wind (cf. Job 6:4), the 'princess' soul hunted, and welfare passing 'as a cloud.'

debates.question: Is the fleeing thing 'my soul' or 'my nobility'?

sides.position: 'My soul' — my princely soul, the noblest part of the man
'My nobility' or dignity — the estate and honour chased away like cloud

themes: the inward turn of the lament

schools.summary: Gill reads the poured-out soul in a rising order — in prayer, in tears, then the very spirits sunk and the soul pouring itself out unto death like a vessel full of holes.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'my soul is poured out within me' of a soul that, yielding to sadness, sinks to its very bottom and flows together in grief.

Henry reads the 'days of affliction' as arresting him like a bailiff, and the soul 'not only weak as water, but lost as water spilt upon the ground' (cf. Ps. 22:14), yet an affliction reckoned by days that heaven has numbered (2 Cor. 4:17).

themes: the low point of the complaint

schools.summary: Gill reads a disease piercing to the bones and marrow in the night, the hour meant for rest, and notes Broughton's 'the night pierced my bones from me.'
Keil and Delitzsch render 'the night rendeth my bones from me, and my gnawers sleep not' — gnawing pains, not resting sinews, that never lie still.
Henry: a sword in his bones, nerves convulsed, sinews taking no rest, so that sleep departed from his eyes.

debates.question: Is the second clause 'my sinews take no rest' or 'my gnawers sleep not,' and who pierces?

sides.position: 'My sinews take no rest' — the disease pierces the bones
'My gnawers sleep not' — gnawing pains that never sleep; the night rends the bones

schools.summary: Gill offers the plainer senses — the garment's colour changed by the running sores, the frequent shifting of raiment, or a garment clinging so close it is changed only with great force.
Clarke reads the 'garment' as the skin, wrapped in an elephantine hide, or the disease seizing him 'as a strong armed man,' throttling him and treading him in the mud.

Keil and Delitzsch take 'garment' strictly, distorted 'by divine omnipotence' and binding like the shirt-collar; Ellicott catalogues both the disfigured skin and the clinging garment, 'by His great power.'

debates.question: What is 'changed' — the literal garment or the diseased skin worn as a garment?

sides.position: The literal garment, disfigured or clinging close
The skin or hide itself, incrusted by the disease

debates.question: Is 'the great force' the violence of the disease or the omnipotence of God?

sides.position: The force of the disease
Divine omnipotence

schools.summary: Gill takes the mire not of sin but of affliction, a man made abject as if flung into a kennel and rolled in it, cast down by a hand he still owns to be God's; he weighs and sets aside the Jewish reading 'it taught me in the mire.'

Ellicott marks the turn 'more directly to God' and the rare phrase 'dust and ashes,' used but three times in Scripture — twice by Job (here and Job 42:6) and once by Abraham (Gen. 18:27); Keil and Delitzsch read God the caster-down.

themes: the phrase of Abraham and of Job's repentance

schools.summary: Gill feels the sharpness of a God who will not hear, or hearing will not answer in the way desired, and reads crying as the vehement language of prayer.

Clarke gathers the whole desolation — persecuted, diseased, forsaken — and reads a God who sees yet does nothing, 'thine eye doth not affect thy heart'; Wesley takes the standing of persevering, importunate prayer.
Ellicott notes the Authorized Version supplies the negative (cf. Ps. 9:18) but records the reading 'thou lookest at me' with mute indifference; Keil and Delitzsch prefer 'thou lookest fixedly at me.'

debates.question: Does the second clause mean 'thou regardest me not,' or 'thou lookest at me' with cold indifference?

sides.position: The negative is supplied: 'thou regardest me not'
'Thou lookest fixedly at me' — God stares with mute indifference

themes: a God who sees and will not stir

schools.summary: Gill owns this 'one of the unbecoming expressions' Job let fall, and answers even as he reports it — God's love to his people is never changed, though his dealings may wear the look of severity.
Keil and Delitzsch render a God who 'changes himself to a cruel being' and 'with the strength of thy hand makest war upon me' — the hand once of blessing now of enmity.

Clarke keeps it to seeming — 'thou appearest to treat me with cruelty... instead of helping, thou opposest me'; Wesley: as if God 'hadst changed thy very nature, which is kind, and merciful, and gracious.'

themes: the strong hand turned to war

schools.summary: Gill reads Job lifted on the wind of affliction and tossed like chaff, though he allows the sense that God raised him high only to cast him lower.
Clarke: stripped of substance, like chaff caught up and dissipated by the wind; Wesley: exposed to every storm, tossed like stubble, his substance and body well-nigh consumed.
Ellicott sets out the choice — a present terror ('thou dissolvest me in thy blast') or a contrast with former honour ('thou usedst to raise me... and now dissolvest my substance,' cf. Ps. 102:10).

debates.question: Does the verse describe present affliction only, or a contrast with former exaltation?

sides.position: Wholly of present affliction — caught up like chaff to be dissolved
A contrast — God once raised him high, now dissolves his substance

schools.summary: Gill takes it of Job's persuasion that this providence will not leave off till it has brought him to the dust, though every man knows death is appointed by the decree of God.

Wesley dwells on the grave as 'the house appointed for all living' — a narrow dark house, yet home and mother's lap, where rich and poor rest; Clarke reads it as the rendezvous of the race and quotes Blair's poem 'The Grave.'

outliers.note: Breaks into a long quotation of Blair's poem 'The Grave,' which personifies death as an insatiable 'great man-eater whose every day is carnival,' still gaping for more.

themes: the house appointed for all living
the grave as home and rest
the settled certainty of the end

schools.summary: Gill reads God's not stretching out his hand to keep Job back from the grave nor fetch him out of it — able, as with the raisings of old, but not so interposing here.

Keil and Delitzsch take it of the falling man's instinct — 'doth not one stretch out the hand in falling, and cry for help in his ruin?'; Ellicott confesses the verse 'hopelessly uncertain,' offering rendering upon rendering.

Clarke and Wesley hear consolation — 'his displeasure shall not proceed beyond the grave'; in the sepulchre is freedom and rest, and though most 'cry in his destruction,' Job fears nothing, 'since I know that my redeemer liveth.'

debates.question: What does this obscure verse mean?

sides.position: God will not reach into the grave to save Job or to keep him there
Even a falling man stretches out his hand and cries for help in his ruin
Beyond the grave God's wrath cannot reach; death is freedom and rest

outliers.note: Declares the verse 'very obscure' and finally 'hopelessly uncertain,' cataloguing several renderings and leaving each reader to make the best sense he can.

themes: the hand stretched out in falling
wrath that stops at the grave

schools.summary: Gill reads a man of tender, sympathizing heart who wept with them that wept — a temper Godlike and Christlike, touched with the feeling of others' infirmities.

Keil and Delitzsch draw out the connective plea — the fellow-feeling Job showed will surely be allowed him in his own misfortune — and gloss 'him that was in trouble' as the hard of lot; Ellicott: Job has not withheld the sympathy for which he now asks in vain.
Clarke records Good's bolder 'should I not weep for the ruthless day?' but keeps the older sense; Wesley hears Job's conscience acquit him — 'I did mourn over others in their miseries.'

debates.question: Does Job weep 'for him that was in trouble,' or (with Good) 'for the ruthless day' of his own calamity?

sides.position: For the sufferer — pleading his past compassion
For the ruthless day — a lament over his own calamity

themes: the plea of a merciful man

schools.summary: Gill draws out the reasonableness of Job's hope — grounded in the covenant kindness of a God who is good and lays up goodness for them that fear him — and the depth of its defeat.

Keil and Delitzsch render the sharp antithesis, 'when I looked for good, then evil came; I waited for light, and darkness came'; Ellicott marks the change from the man of ch. 3:25 who braced for the worst to one who hoped for the best and was deceived.
Wesley keeps it personal — 'yet trouble came upon myself, when I expected it not.'
Gill weighs the boiling of the inward parts both ways — a literal fever burning within, or the seething of a mind under great distress — and lets both stand.

Clarke hears the commotion every humane person feels at the sight of misery, tying the verse back to Job's own compassion; Wesley: affliction 'came upon me suddenly and unexpectedly, when I promised myself peace.'
Ellicott would render it present — 'my bowels boil, and rest not; days of affliction have overtaken me unawares.'
Henry: the sense of calamity preying continually on his spirits, the days of affliction 'preventing' him without previous warning.

themes: bowels that boil and rest not

schools.summary: Gill offers 'out of the sun' in mourning black, or 'I go black, but not by the sun' — his skin darkened by disease, not sunburn, like a dweller in Kedar's tents.
Clarke widens the dispute: the word may mean 'without a protector,' or (from a root for heat) 'without fury,' the Vulgate's and Calmet's 'deep sadness, but no angry spirit.'

Ellicott prefers 'without the sun' and notes Job cried 'not merely in secret but in the face of all men'; Keil and Delitzsch take the word strictly of the mourner's dirty-black dress, not the leper's skin.
Henry catches the public shame: in the congregation Job could not stand up calmly but 'stood up and cried aloud,' like one half distracted.

sides.position: He went mourning deprived of the sun's light and comfort, in mourner's black
'Blackened, but not by the sun' — his skin darkened by disease
'Without a protector,' or 'without fury/anger'

schools.summary: Gill gathers the senses of the kinship — dwelling among the venomous, likeness in solitude, or mournful notes like their unpitied cry — and notes the versions' 'ostriches.'
Clarke fixes the resemblance in the cry — the jackals or hyenas and the 'daughters of howling,' remarkable for their mournful voice; Wesley: 'a brother by imitation of their cries.'
Ellicott gives 'jackals and ostriches' for the moderns; Keil and Delitzsch so render, and mark this the first plain mention of Job's leprosy.
Henry holds both strands — brother to these creatures in choosing solitude (Isa. 34:13) and in his hideous, inarticulate cries.

debates.question: Are the creatures 'dragons and owls' or 'jackals and ostriches'?

sides.position: Dragons and owls
Jackals and ostriches (the moderns)

themes: the mournful cry of the waste

schools.summary: Gill reads the blackened skin of melancholy or, more likely, of the burning ulcers and black scabs that covered him as famine blackens its victims.
Clarke takes the black skin of exposure to the parching sun and 'the bones burned with heat' as the raging fever preying on his vitals.
Keil and Delitzsch render a skin that, become black, 'peels off from me,' and bones consumed and set in a glow — the first plain mention of the leprosy.
Henry gathers it into one grim image: skin black, sores scabbed, bones burnt with a constant fever drying the marrow — 'see how frail our bodies are.'
Gill recalls Job's harp used as David's, in worship or innocent recreation, now wholly laid aside, so that nothing is heard but the voice of mourning.

Keil and Delitzsch hear the poet let the whole monologue die away in prolonged elegiac strains, the cheerful music (Job 21:12) turned to sobbing; Ellicott renders the stringed and wind instruments (cf. Gen. 4:21) turned to mourning.

Clarke: Job's only music now is his plaintive cries, and the chapter, for all its sorrow, is tempered with a calmness not seen before the confession of ch. 19:25, after which Job 'mourned not without hope.'
